title: Research Bite #26: Interleaving Retrieval Practice Promotes Science Learning
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #26 covers Sana and Yan's Psychological Science study on interleaved retrieval practice in high-school science classrooms. The researchers compared weekly quizzes that mixed questions from different concepts (interleaved) against quizzes that grouped questions by concept (blocked) and against unquizzed material, then tested retention a month later. Interleaved quizzes felt harder in the moment -- students scored slightly worse on them than on blocked quizzes -- but produced significantly better retention and conceptual understanding on the delayed final test, outperforming both blocked quizzes and no quizzing at all. The mechanism the authors point to is discrimination: mixing concepts forces students to actively distinguish between them rather than coast on short-term contextual cues, which is exactly the kind of durable, transferable learning teachers want. Because the intervention only required reordering existing quiz questions -- not rebuilding curriculum or writing new material -- Barton flags it as a low-cost, high-leverage change: teachers can interleave using assignments, test banks, and end-of-chapter problems they already have, simply by changing the sequence.
points: Interleaved quizzes produced significantly better one-month retention and conceptual understanding than blocked quizzes, despite scoring slightly lower in the moment -- a clear case of a "desirable difficulty."
The mechanism is discrimination: mixing concepts forces students to actively distinguish between them rather than lean on short-term contextual cues from a blocked sequence.
The intervention is genuinely low-cost: teachers can interleave using their existing assignments, test banks, and end-of-chapter questions just by resequencing them, without new material.
The one-month delayed testing window makes this one of the stronger demonstrations that interleaving benefits are durable, not just an artifact of immediate post-quiz measurement.
quotes: This research article in Psychological Science investigates the impact of interleaved retrieval practice on science learning in high school students.

Findings revealed that while interleaved quizzes were initially more challenging, they led to significantly better retention and conceptual understanding on a final test one month later compared to blocked quizzes and unquizzed material.

Interleaving forces learners to discriminate between concepts, enhancing their conceptual understanding. The study found that interleaved quizzes led to even greater learning gains than blocked quizzes.

Teachers can likely use their existing assignments, test banks, and end-of-chapter problems and simply change the order of questions to incorporate interleaving. This makes the strategy cost-effective and not overly time-intensive.

The positive effects of interleaved retrieval practice were observed on a surprise test administered one month after the quizzing period, indicating that this strategy can lead to sustained learning benefits.
These results demonstrate a cost-effective strategy to promote classroom learning
